info.disambiguation: American singer and actor, “Ol’ Blue Eyes”
info.bio:
Francis Albert Sinatra (Hoboken, 12 de diciembre de 1915 - Los Ángeles, 14 de mayo de 1998), Frank Sinatra, La voz, cantante y actor estadounidense.

Considerado entre los mejores cantantes populares de la historia, su repertorio se basa en la obra de los más importantes compositores populares estadounidenses (Cole Porter, Sammy Cahn, George Gershwin ...) y su categoría artística se fundamenta en unas cualidades interpretativas que le permiten transmitir las emociones y sentimientos implícitos en las letras de las canciones.

scenes.name: El pop de papá y mamá
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los adultos compraban LPs (a 32 chelines frente a los 6 de un single) y también muchos singles, de modo que la lista británica de 1965 era esquizofrénica: los Stones y los Beatles competían con lo que los adolescentes llamaban «música de papás y mamás», Ken Dodd, los Seekers, los Bachelors o Jim Reeves. La banda sonora de The Sound of Music encabezó la lista de LPs casi todo 1965 y 1966. Los adolescentes más jóvenes encontraban nuevos ídolos como los Walker Brothers, baladistas melodramáticos a lo Spector.

scenes.name: Frankie Crocker y WBLS
scenes.book: The Come Up: An Oral History of the Rise of Hip-Hop
scenes.author: Jonathan Abrams
scenes.desc: El director de programación de WBLS-FM disparó la audiencia con el formato urban contemporary: disco, R&B, rock y luego hip hop sin etiquetas raciales, de Madonna a Hall & Oates. Era el maestro de ceremonias carismático cuyas rimas imitarían los MCs, y despedía cada noche con «Moody’s Mood for Love». Receloso del relevo, no negó la popularidad del hip hop: puso algunos de sus primeros discos y fichó a Mr. Magic. «No sé si el hip hop habría pasado en Nueva York sin Frankie Crocker» (Bill Stephney).

scenes.name: Casa Loma, Dorsey, Shaw y Miller: las big bands blancas
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Antes de Goodman, la Casa Loma Orchestra (cooperativa salida de Goldkette, dirigida por Glen Gray, arreglos de Gene Gifford) conquista los campus con tempos frenéticos y secciones impecables: los jóvenes empiezan a dictar el gusto musical y la música se vuelve un «estilo de vida». Bob Crosby lleva el Dixieland a la big band; Tommy Dorsey, tras pelearse con su hermano Jimmy, acumula éxitos («Marie», «Song of India», un joven Frank Sinatra) y se vuelve más swing con Sy Oliver. Artie Shaw, «rey del clarinete», rival elegante y frío de Goodman, ocho veces casado, triunfa con «Begin the Beguine» y contrata a Billie Holiday y Roy Eldridge. Glenn Miller cierra el ciclo con riffs fáciles y melodías pegadizas («Moonlight Serenade», «In the Mood») que anuncian la música popular de posguerra. La huelga de Petrillo (1942-1944), la guerra y el propio agotamiento del swing acaban con la época más que el bebop.

podcast.title: Transition from Big Band Singer to Solo Star (1942)
podcast.body: Frank Sinatra, like other big band singers, benefited from the loophole in the 1942 American Federation of Musicians strike. Not being categorized as "musicians" by the union, these singers were free to record and embark on solo careers, becoming stars in their own right, independent of band leaders. "And names included Bing Crosby and Frank Sinatra and Perry Como, all former big band singers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Conspicuous Presence at First Grammys (1959)
podcast.body: Frank Sinatra was the "most conspicuous presence" at the first Grammy Awards ceremony held in May 1959 at the Beverly Hilton Hotel, where he notably bought two tables for his Rat Pack friends. Despite high expectations, being nominated for five Grammys, he left with only an album packaging award. "Cruelling legend Frank Sinatra was the most conspicuous presence. He'd bought two tables for his rat-packed friends."

podcast.title: Grammy Snub at First Ceremony (1959)
podcast.body: Despite being nominated for five Grammys, including two for Album of the Year and Record of the Year for "Witchcraft," Frank Sinatra "came away with almost nothing" at the inaugural Grammys in 1959, winning only an album packaging award and no performance Grammys. He was reportedly "furious." "But that night, Sinatra came away with almost nothing, winning only an album packaging award for his LP Only The Lonely, and not a single performance Grammy."

podcast.title: Early Microphone Singer
podcast.body: Frank Sinatra is identified as one of the performers who emerged with the advent of electrical recording and the microphone. This technology allowed singers to adopt a more nuanced style, singing softly and romantically, which led to the term "microphone singers" and later "crooners." "This is where we get performers like Frank Sinatra and Bing Crosby."

podcast.body: Frank Sinatra was cited as an example of an artist with "parallel careers in the cinema and in music," a path that Elvis Presley hoped to emulate with his own film career. podcast.title: Strike-Proof Vocalist
podcast.body: During the Musicians' Union Strike of 1942-44, which prohibited instrumentalists from recording for major labels, singers like Frank Sinatra were unaffected. As Tommy Dorsey's old vocalist, he was able to continue recording, backed by vocal groups instead of instrumentalists. This period contributed to the rise of singers as stars in American music, shifting away from instrumentalists. "Dorsi's old vocalist Frank Sinatra could, backed by a vocal group instead of instrumentalists."

podcast.title: Symbol of "Real Music" (1960s)
podcast.body: During the decline of rock and roll in the early 1960s, many record executives declared rock a mere fad and suggested a return to "real music" with "real artists" like Frank Sinatra. "Conventional wisdom was that everybody could go back to making real music with real artists like Frank Sinatra."

podcast.title: Target of Screaming Fans
podcast.body: Frank Sinatra became a significant target of screaming female fans in the generation following Rudy Vallée. This "screaming mania" continued a pattern of intense fan devotion to popular male singers, preceding the phenomenon later seen with The Beatles. "The next generation, the daughters of Valley fans, latched onto Frank Sinatra, and the grand daughters became screaming Beetlemaniacs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocal Coaching Influence
podcast.body: During the recording of Joy Division's "Closer" album, Ian Curtis was made to listen extensively to Frank Sinatra records by producer Martin Hannett and Tony Wilson. This unusual coaching technique was aimed at helping Ian develop a deeper, richer, and more authoritative vocal delivery, which contributed to the album's haunting sound. "Why? Because they made him listen to a lot of Frank Sinatra records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Vocal Style Avoiding Malisma
podcast.body: Sinatra is cited as one of the great voices of the first part of the 20th century who, almost without exception, would hit the note "dead arm" with one note per syllable, eschewing ornamentation and frills, which was considered good singing at the time. "If you listen to any of the great voices of the first part of the 20th century, Sinatra, Bing Crosby, Tony Bennett, they will almost without exception hit the note dead arm, one note per syllable."

"The next generation, the daughters of Valley fans, latched onto Frank Sinatra, and the grand daughters became screaming Beetlemaniacs."

xref.title: Tony Wilson's Vocal Suggestion
xref.body: Tony Wilson of Factory Records suggested to Ian Curtis that he try using his baritone range when singing "Love Will Tear Us Apart," in a manner similar to Frank Sinatra. Curtis adopted this suggestion, adding a "very old-school crooning" element to his vocal performance on the track. "Tony Wilson of the band's factory records made a suggestion. Ian tried using the baritone range in the same way Frank Sinatra would when you sing this song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Voice Transformation for 'Closer'
xref.body: During the recording of the "Closer" album in March 1980, producer Martin Hannett and Factory Records head Tony Wilson coached Ian to achieve a deeper and richer vocal delivery by having him listen extensively to Frank Sinatra records, which resulted in a more haunting and authoritative sound that made his portrayals of pain and alienation highly credible. "Why? Because they made him listen to a lot of Frank Sinatra records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Ziggy Stardust Persona
xref.body: Bowie immersed himself fully into the persona of Ziggy Stardust, a "doomed pansexual alien." This character was a "pre-packaged synthetic ultra glamorous, ultra theatrical, fantastical rock star" that fundamentally changed the presentation of rock music. "Bowie immersed himself into this new persona, this doomed pansexual alien, and he invented a new name for himself. It was Ziggy Stardust."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
